extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP scholars, and law students interested in enablement and antibody patents
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-academic analysis of the enablement and written-description doctrines after Amgen v. Sanofi, with particular attention to antibody patents, claim forms (structural/functional/genus), key case law, and technological implications (e.g., AI/protein folding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. §112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using it 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art ... to make and use the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure must enable a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) to make and use the full scope of what is claimed. The article repeatedly cites the statutory text and explains that enablement is not satisfied unless the full claimed scope is taught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (separate from enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must 'describe an invention understandable to that skilled artisan and show that the inventor actually invented the invention claimed.' (Ariad / Federal Circuit)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description is judged by whether the specification shows the inventor possessed the claimed invention. It is distinct from enablement (which addresses making/using). Courts examine whether the spec 'adequately describes' the claimed subject matter; lacking this, claims can be invalid even if enabling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode disclosure (historical statutory component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112 historically required disclosure of the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention; AIA left the disclosure but removed penalties for failing to satisfy the best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the article notes Congress left disclosure requirements intact, the America Invents Act removed enforcement penalties for failure to disclose best mode—practical impact and continued relevance may be limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim particularity and definiteness (35 U.S.C. §112(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must 'particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor ... regards as the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define the metes-and-bounds of the monopoly; drafters seek breadth but must remain within what the specification supports. Overbroad or vague claiming risks invalidation under the disclosure requirements and other doctrines (e.g., indefiniteness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural claims (what to disclose for structure-based claiming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that describe the elements of an invention in relation to each other and their arrangement (example: bicycle pulley components).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural claims disclose elements and interactions so a PHOSITA can construct the invention; when structure is disclosed, enablement is generally straightforward for those embodiments described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claims / means-plus-function (§112(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: An element may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without reciting structure, but the claim is construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claiming allows describing results rather than structure, but patent scope is limited to the structures (and equivalents) actually disclosed in the specification. The statutory text governs; courts construe such claims to the corresponding disclosed structure and equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims and the 'quality common' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus claims cover species sharing a common attribute or property; to validly claim a genus an inventor must identify a 'quality common' to all members that distinguishes them and is adapted to the claimed use (Incandescent Lamp).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (e.g., Incandescent Lamp) will invalidate genus claims if the specification only discloses a few species without showing the common characteristic across the claimed genus; broad genus claims must teach how to select/identify members of the genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: O’Reilly v. Morse principle (no claiming all manifestations without disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor cannot claim an entire technology or 'every mode' of accomplishing a result unless the specification enables all such manifestations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morse's eighth claim (claiming all uses of galvanic current) was invalidated because it claimed far more than Morse had described/enabled. Anti-pattern: claiming a broad result without teaching how to achieve all implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full-scope enablement test
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent's specification must enable the full scope of the invention as defined by its claims; enablement must cover the full range claimed without undue experimentation (endorsed by Amgen and earlier Federal Circuit cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate whether the disclosure teaches how to make and use the full claimed range; claiming a broad parameter or range without enabling embodiments across that range risks invalidation (illustrated by MagSil, Idenix, and Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: In re Wands undue experimentation factors (eight-factor test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors used to evaluate whether practicing the invention over the full scope would require undue experimentation: (1) quantity of experimentation necessary, (2) amount of direction/guidance presented, (3) presence/absence of working examples, (4) nature of the invention, (5) state of the prior art, (6) relative skill of those in the art, (7) predictability/unpredictability of the art, and (8) breadth of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These eight Wands factors are weighed holistically; presence of working examples, clear guidance, predictable art, and narrower claim breadth favor enablement. Cases apply these factors to determine whether experimentation is 'undue.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability of the art and PHOSITA skill are central considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement analysis depends critically on how predictable the field is and what a PHOSITA can do given the specification and prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fields that are unpredictable (e.g., novel biotech) make broad claims harder to enable; courts consider the PHOSITA's skill level and available prior art in assessing whether undue experimentation would be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description: proof of possession (showing actual invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must show that the inventor 'actually invented' the claimed invention—mere statement of desired result or function without description of the invention is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for descriptions (e.g., sequences, structures, working examples) that demonstrate possession of the claimed invention. Anti-pattern: claiming a genus based on functional description alone without species or structural detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibody-specific enablement issues (the 'antibody exception' and its decline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, courts applied a lower enablement/written-description standard to antibody patents (the antibody exception / newly characterized antigen test), treating antibodies functionally; Amgen rejects tech-exceptionalism and applies the full-scope enablement test to antibodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because antibodies are often conceived functionally (many antibodies can bind the same antigen), courts previously allowed broader claims based on functional teaching; Amgen realigns antibody enablement with statutory text—patents must enable the full claimed genus or provide sufficient species/structural disclosure (e.g., sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-law examples applying full-scope enablement (MagSil, Idenix, Amgen)
rubrics_metrics.description: MagSil invalidated claims that claimed resistive change ranges not enabled by the specification; Idenix invalidated claims requiring screening of many candidate compounds; Amgen held antibody genus claims invalid for lack of enablement of full scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These decisions illustrate how courts apply the full-scope/undue-experimentation principles: claims encompassing large unexplained ranges or requiring massive screening are vulnerable. Examples provide practical indicators (e.g., claimed ranges vs. disclosed achievements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical disclosure strategies to meet enablement for broad coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: To enable broader scopes, applicants can (a) disclose species/working examples (e.g., sequences), (b) provide clear methods and guidance for making/using embodiments, (c) disclose predictive correlations/common quality for the genus, or (d) enumerate many species (e.g., listing many sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article discusses hypotheticals where AI could allow listing large numbers of sequences (10,000) or providing AI model inputs/training data as a way to enable broad genus claims. Tradeoffs include USPTO/examiner workload and potential written-description/utility questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy principle: quid pro quo — monopoly in exchange for teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental patent rationale requires balancing claim scope with the disclosure given; patents grant limited monopolies so long as the public receives sufficient teaching to practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This normative principle underlies enablement/written-description doctrine and motivates courts to invalidate claims that claim more than the disclosure justifies (preventing 'taking more benefit than given').

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal aspect of enablement (judged as of filing date)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement and written description are assessed based on what the specification and the art taught as of the patent's filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not always spelled out in a single sentence on the excerpt, the article's case discussions (e.g., Wands, MagSil) assume enablement is measured at filing — applicants cannot rely on later-developed techniques to cure inadequacies in disclosure at filing.
